KS Express Boilerplate

A Visual Studio Code extension that generates an Express.js starter project from the Explorer right-click menu, so you don't have to build the same folders and files by hand every time.

Publisher: KeshavSoft Marketplace ID: ks-express-boilerplate Version 1.10.2 MIT License
Install from Marketplace GitHub Repository
Introduction

What it is

KS Express Boilerplate is a Visual Studio Code extension published by KeshavSoft. Once installed, it adds a set of commands to the Explorer right-click menu. You right-click a folder, choose what you want to generate, and the extension writes a ready-to-run Express.js project into that folder — the entry file, the router, the configuration, and the server startup.

Everything it produces is plain Node.js and Express. There is no separate framework and nothing hidden: the generated files are ordinary JavaScript you can read, edit, and run.

Why it exists

The first part of nearly every Express project is the same repetitive setup — creating folders, wiring up Express, adding a router, and preparing configuration. This extension exists to remove that repetition, so you can start from a working structure instead of an empty folder.

Who it is for

It is aimed at developers who create Express projects often, developers building CRUD APIs, and people learning how a backend project should be organized. Anyone who wants a faster, more consistent start for an Express application will get use out of it.

The problem

The repetitive work it removes

Starting an Express project sounds simple, but in practice the first phase is repetitive and time-consuming. Before writing any real business logic, developers usually repeat the same steps:

  • Initialize npm and install Express
  • Create the folder structure — deciding where routes, config, and public files go
  • Write the server startup and port handling
  • Set up environment files and a configuration loader
  • Create the routing skeleton, again

On one project this is a minor annoyance. Across many projects it adds up, and for someone still learning backend structure it is a source of inconsistency — routes, config, and server code end up arranged differently every time, which makes each project harder to maintain.

The idea: replace that manual setup with a single menu action that always produces the same clean structure.

Features

What the extension provides

The extension contributes three commands, all available from the Explorer right-click menu when you right-click a folder:

Menu command What it does
Express BoilerPlate with simple Generates a simple Express project into the selected folder.
Express BoilerPlate with simple crud functionality Generates a simple Express project that also includes CRUD functionality.
Express BoilerPlate Templates Opens a panel where you can generate Express templates for different use cases.
🖱️

Right-click generation

Create a project straight from the Explorer context menu — no terminal commands to type.

📁

Consistent structure

Each generated project uses the same organized layout, with config, public, and API kept separate.

🔌

Pre-wired entry file

The generated app.js already loads config, mounts routes, and starts the server.

🧩

Template panel

The Templates command opens a panel to generate different starting points for different use cases.

🌐

Optional browser open

The generated entry file can open the app in your browser when OPEN_BROWSER is set to true.

🚀

Ready to run

The output is plain Node and Express, so the project runs without any extra setup.

Quick Start

Get Started in Minutes

  1. Install the extension from the VS Code Marketplace.
  2. Open VS Code Explorer.
  3. Right-click any folder.
  4. Select one of the available Express BoilerPlate commands.
  5. Wait for the project generation.
  6. Open the generated project and start development.
Installation

Installing the extension

The extension is installed from the Visual Studio Code Marketplace.

  1. Open Visual Studio Code.
  2. Open the Extensions view and search for ks-express-boilerplate by publisher KeshavSoft, or open the Marketplace page directly.
  3. Click Install.
What you see
The extension’s page inside VS Code, showing the publisher (KeshavSoft) and the install controls. Here it is already installed, so the button reads Uninstall.
Why it matters
Installing this extension is what adds the generator commands to the Explorer menu. Without it, the commands in the next steps do not appear.
Expected result
After installing, the extension is active and its commands are available the next time you right-click a folder in the Explorer.
Step-by-step

Generating a project

The screenshots below follow one project from the right-click menu to a generated, runnable backend. Each step explains what you are looking at, why it matters, what the extension is doing, and the expected result.

1

Right-click a folder to open the commands

Open the folder where you want the project, then right-click it in the Explorer. The extension’s commands appear in the context menu.

What you see
The Explorer context menu with three commands added near the top: Express BoilerPlate Templates, Express BoilerPlate with simple, and Express BoilerPlate with simple crud functionality.
Why it matters
This menu is the entry point for the whole workflow. It replaces opening a terminal and running setup commands by hand.
What the extension does
These commands are registered against folders, so they only appear when you right-click a folder in the Explorer.
Expected result
Choosing one of the three commands starts generation into the folder you right-clicked.
2

Choose a template from the Templates panel

Selecting Express BoilerPlate Templates opens a panel with template options for different use cases.

What you see
A panel (titled BoilerPlate) with an Actions area listing three template cards: sendWithMail, tallyServer, and labManagement. Each card generates its corresponding boilerplate.
Why it matters
This is where you pick which template to generate. Different actions produce different starting points, so you choose the one that fits your use case.
What the extension does
When you click an action, the extension copies that template’s boilerplate into the folder you started from.
Expected result
The selected template is generated, and the panel reports that generation is complete.
3

The generated project appears

The folder is now a complete Express project, and a notification confirms it was created.

What you see
A populated Explorer containing .vscode, Config, Public, environment files, and the core JavaScript files — plus a notification confirming success.
Why it matters
This is the structure you would otherwise create by hand. It arrives already organized and consistent.
What the extension does
It writes the template’s folders and files into your workspace and shows a confirmation message when finished.
Expected result
A success message such as “Node API initialized successfully” and a ready project. Each file is explained in Generated project structure.
4

The generated app.js

The application entry point is generated already wired together — you do not have to connect anything before running it.

Generated app.js
import { exec } from "child_process";
import express from "express";
import loadConfig from "./configLoader.js";
import setupRoutes from "./routes.js";
import startServer from "./server.js";

loadConfig();

const app = express()

setupRoutes(app);

const { port } = startServer(app);

if (process.env.OPEN_BROWSER === "true") {
    exec(`start http://localhost:${port}`);
};
What you see
app.js in the editor. It imports Express, the config loader, the routes module, and the server module, then wires them together.
Why it matters
The wiring between Express, configuration, routes, and the server is the error-prone part of setup. Here it is generated correctly and the same way every time.
What the extension does
It generates an entry file that calls loadConfig(), creates the app, runs setupRoutes(app), and starts the server with startServer(app). If OPEN_BROWSER is true, it opens the app in your browser.
Expected result
A runnable entry file. You can start the server and then build your own logic on top of it.
5

The generated routes file

The router is where your endpoints will live. It is generated and exported, ready for you to add routes.

Generated routes.js
import express from 'express';

const router = express.Router();

export { router };
What you see
routes.js in the editor — an Express router created and exported. For this template it is placed under an Api folder.
Why it matters
Endpoints stay in their own file, separate from server setup, so you add routes here without touching the entry file.
What the extension does
It generates a router module (express.Router()) and exports it, and app.js imports and mounts it through setupRoutes.
Expected result
A working router you can extend right away. This is where your own development begins.
The output

Generated project structure

A generated project uses the layout below. Each item has a clear job, which is what keeps the structure readable and consistent from one project to the next. 

# Generated Express project
project-folder/
├── .vscode/            # editor settings for the project
├── Config/             # configuration files
├── Public/             # static files and UI pages
├── .env                # environment variables
├── .env.local          # local environment overrides
├── app.js              # entry point: config + routes + server
├── config.json         # configuration values
├── configLoader.js     # loads configuration (used by app.js)
├── package-lock.json   # locked dependency versions
├── package.json        # project dependencies and metadata
├── port.js             # port handling
├── routes.js           # the router, mounted by app.js
└── server.js           # server startup (used by app.js)

The app.js file ties the project together: it imports configLoader.js, routes.js, and server.js, calls each in turn, and starts the server. The key idea is separation — configuration, routing, and server startup each live in their own file. Depending on the template you generate, the router may be placed under an Api folder, as shown in the walkthrough.

Benefits

Why it helps

  • Consistency. Every generated project uses the same structure, so moving between projects is straightforward.
  • Time saved. The setup that normally takes 15–30 minutes of manual work is done in a few seconds from the menu.
  • Reduced setup effort. No repeated npm init, no re-typing the same server and routing code, no manual folder creation.
  • Standardized project structure. Configuration, routing, and server startup are separated the same way each time.
  • Beginner friendly. Developers learning Express get a sensible, working layout to study and build on, instead of guessing where things belong.

Freelancers

Spin up a consistent starting point quickly across many client projects.

Anyone creating Express projects

Begin from a ready, organized base instead of an empty folder.

Conclusion

Summary

KS Express Boilerplate turns the repetitive setup at the start of an Express project into a single right-click. You pick one of its commands — a simple project, a simple project with CRUD, or a template from the Templates panel — and the extension generates a complete, consistently organized Express project into your folder, with the entry file, router, configuration, and server already wired together.

The result is less time spent on foundations and more time spent on the actual work: writing your endpoints and building your application.
